Experimental methodology
Materials and synthesis
Nickel oxide and its doped variations with chromium, copper, or iron were fabricated through the co-precipitation 
method. The chemicals used in this study were of high purity and were used as they were without any additional 
purification  processes.  The  precursor  materials  used  in  this  study  were  obtained  from  Merck  company  and 
included  the  following:  Nickel  (II)  nitrate  hexahydrate  (Ni(NO3)2.6H2O)  (CAS#:13,478–00-7),  Chromium 
(III) nitrate nonahydrate (Cr(NO3)3•9H2O) (CAS#:7789–02-8), Copper nitrate trihydrate (Cu(NO3)2•3H2O) 
(CAS#:10,031–43-3), and Iron (III) chloride hexahydrate (FeCl3•6H2O) (CAS#:0250-03943-1). For synthesizing 
0.5 M NiO nanoparticles, 14.54 g of nickel nitrate hexahydrate [Ni (NO3)26H2O] was added to 100 ml water 
which is distilled and stirred in a beaker at a temperature of 80 degrees for 30 min. Then, ammonia solution was 
added slowly (in drops) until a green precipitate formed and the pH value was adjusted to 10. Ammonia solution 
is used as a reduction agent. The resultant solution was stirred at the same temperature for 2 h, followed by 
several rinse with ethanol and water to attain a neutral pH of 7. To obtain NiO powder, the precipitate from the 
final solution was dried and calcined at 600 degree for 4 h. On the other hand, for preparation of doped samples, 
the  Co-precipitation  method  was  used  as  follows:  a  100  cc  amount  of  0.5  M  Nickel  (II)  nitrate  hexahydrate 
solution is poured into a beaker and stirred for 30 min when it becomes uniform, Fe, Cu, and Cr (5%w) solution 
was added to it. After 30 min, 1 M NaOH solution was added to the final product drop by drop for 1 h until the 
pH value was adjusted to 10. Then it is stirred for 2 h at a temperature of 80 degrees until a precipitate is formed. 
The resultant precipitate is washed and dried in an oven for 16 h and calcined in the furnace. The calcination 
temperature of each dope was different: Fe: 850 ◦C, Cu: 550 ◦C and Cr: 700 ◦C Fig. 1 and 2 clearly illustrate the 
synthesis structure of the materials at a glance 31–33.

Given that the treatment temperature can influence the crystal structure and size of nanoparticles during 
the synthesis process, and considering that the size, shape, and crystal structure of the particles affect the optical 
performance. In this study to produce nanoparticles affected with better optical performance and to remove 
moisture  and  convert  hydroxide  to  metal  oxide,  testing,  and  optimization  were  conducted  at  a  temperature 
of 500 to 850◦ C. Within this range of temperatures, specific temperatures that exhibited appropriate optical 
behavior in nanoparticles were chosen to enable comparison of the resulting samples. Moreover, by optimizing 
the temperature in this process, ie, considering the low doping percentage of the elements, the different doping 
were distinguished from each other. These temperatures are the usual ones used in previous works (Fe: 850 ℃, 
Cu: 550 ℃ and Cr: 700 ℃ )35,36 .

physical and chemical characteristics of metal oxide nanostructures, the nonlinear optical characteristics in such 
substances remain insufficiently realized. These NLO properties depend on the properties of the nanoparticles

semiconductor with energy of band gap between 3.6 and 4 eV8, is a hopeful nonlinear optical (NLO) substance 
due to the high laser damage, NLO coefficient, and widespread transparency9. NiO has found applications in 
diverse  fields,  including  catalysis,  battery  cathodes,  gas  sensors,  electrochromic  films,  and  dye-sensitized 
photocathodes10,11,12,13.  Moreover,  engineering  efforts  have  been  directed  towards  the  synthesis  of  NiO 
nanoparticles to attain ferromagnetism (FM) suitable for spintronic applications14. In Advanced Photonics, NiO 
thin films with nonlinear optical characteristic are under investigation and play a fundamental role in memory 
components, switches, and absorbers15. Many studies have explored the NLO characteristics of NiO thin films 
by varying dopants and their respective concentrations15–23. Their exceptional nonlinear optical reactin, coupled 
with  rapid  reaction  times,  positions  them  as  promising  candidates  for  applications  in  optical  limiting  and 
switching. Notably, Pepe et al.24 have also contributed to this field of research. Synthesized Cr/Sb-doped NiO 
nanoparticles through a hydrothermal technique and obtained a nonlinear absorption coefficient of 1.84 × 10⁻4 
cm/W, which rise to 7.45 × 10⁻4 cm/W and 4.18 × 10⁻4 cm/W with Cr and Sb doping, respectively. These findings 
emphasize the potential of NiO, NiO: Cr, and NiO: Sb nanocomposite films as optical limiters in optoelectronic 
applications  owing  to  their  low  thresholds25.  On  the  other  hand,  the  surface  imperfections  inherent  in 
nanostructures  markedly  influence  their  physical  and  chemical  properties,  which  can  be  evaluated  through 
nonlinear optical (NLO) experiments. Gaining a comprehensive insight into the defect states and their impact 
on NLO properties is crucial for designing and manufacturing effective optical limiters. For this reason, an ideal 
optical limiter would serve to safeguard both human vision and sensorial optical instruments from high-intensity 
laser radiation26. Researchers used the spray pyrolysis technique to create NiO and NiO: Cu thin films (with Cu 
concentrations ranging from 0.1% to 25%) on soda-lime glass substrates. They investigated the optical properties 
and electrical resistivity of these films. Notably, the optical band gap decreased with increasing Cu/Ni ratio, while 
the  index  of  refraction  and  Urbach  energy  enhanced.  The  films  exhibited  good  optical  response,  and  their 
photoluminescence spectra showed distinct peaks. Additionally, electrical resistivity decreased with higher Cu 
content27. NiO nanostructured thin films doped with varying concentrations of Fe were fabricated using a simple 
spin-coating  method. The  films  exhibited  good  crystallinity  along  the  (111)  plane  and  were  confirmed  to  be 
single-phase NiO by X-ray method. With increasing Fe content, the crystallite size decreased from 36 to 8 nm. 
Optical studies revealed high transparency (70–85%) and a direct energy gap about 3.60 to 3.64 eV for different 
Fe: NiO compositions. Nonlinear properties, including χ1, χ3, and n₂, improved significantly due to Fe doping, 
enhancing  their  potential  for  optoelectronic  applications21.  Utilized  the  nanosecond  Z-scan  technique  to

devices28. The Z-scan technique was employed to study the nonlinear optical properties of VS2 and VS2/MoS2 
nanocomposites, revealing a transition from saturable absorption in VS2 to reverse saturable absorption in the 
composite.  This  method  provided  insights  into  phase  shifts  and  changes  in  the  nonlinear  refractive  index, 
indicating  significant  potential  for  optical  device  applications29.  In  another  study  examines  the  electronic 
structures  of  silicon  under  strain  using  a  supercell  model,  revealing  that  band  folding  can  mislead  the 
identification of bandgap transitions. Specifically, it corrects the claim of an indirect-to-direct bandgap transition 
at 4% strain along the Si(110) orientation, showing instead that the conduction band minimum shifts without 
such a transition30. Based on the literature, the nanopowders with NiO, CuNiO, CrNiO and FeNiO configurations 
are  designed  explicitly  for  photocatalysis  and  electronic  applications.  In  previous  investigations,  we  have

of  NiO  and  NiO  nanopowders  doped  with  Cu,  Cr,  and  Fe.  A  review  of  existing  literature  reveals  a  notable 
deficiency  in  comprehensive  comparative  analyses  utilizing  the  Z-scan  approach  to  evaluate  the  nonlinear 
optical (NLO) properties exhibited by NiO, CuNiO, CrNiO, and FeNiO nanopowders. Moreover, there appears 
to be an absence of dedicated research focusing specifically on the NLO characteristics of these compounds. 
Consequently, this research aims to pioneer an exploration of their NLO properties through the application of 
the Z-scan approach. The methodology of synthesis is of paramount significance in the context of metallic oxide

pH value was adjusted to 10. Then it is stirred for 2 h at a temperature of 80 degrees until a precipitate is formed. 
The resultant precipitate is washed and dried in an oven for 16 h and calcined in the furnace. The calcination 
temperature of each dope was different: Fe: 850 ◦C, Cu: 550 ◦C and Cr: 700 ◦C Fig. 1 and 2 clearly illustrate the

The data in Table 1 show that doping (Cu and Cr) in the NiO structure led to an increase and iron doping led

the elevated values of dislocation density δ and ϵ for the Cr-doped NiO sample (as shown in Table 1) confirm a 
more significant structural disorder or crystal imperfections, which contribute to diminished crystallinity and 
reduced crystallite dimensions45,46. Table 1 illustrates that the crystallite size of pristine NiO increases with the 
incorporation of Fe dopants. The minor variations in lattice parameters can be attributed to discrepancies in 
ionic radii. Dislocation density display the number of lattice defects within the sample. When interstitial sites 
are occupied, it can lead to an expansion of the lattice parameters. Conversely, the formation of oxygen vacancies 
or the oxidation of Ni2 + to Ni3 + in the doped samples can lead to modifications in the lattice parameter, as 
Ni3 + has a smaller radius than Ni2 + , and oxygen vacancies possess a radius that is smaller than that of lattice 
oxygen. Moreover, a reduced crystallite size is associated with an enhancement of grain boundary effects and 
an increased prevalence imperfections of lattice, as evidenced by the density displacement (δ) calculated from 
Eq. (4) refer to Table 147,48. Furthermore, the broadening of the peaks is exacerbated by various doping elements, 
which suggests a reduction in the size of the crystallites, except for iron doping, the size of which was estimated 
using the Scherrer formula. It is evident that the values of the lattice parameter 'a' are significantly influenced by 
doping49,50. The structural changes observed upon doping in the NiO lattice, such as variations in dislocation 
density  and  crystallite  size,  are  critical  for  understanding  the  material’s  physical  properties.  The  increase  in 
dislocation  density  with  Cr  and  Cu  doping  indicates  a  rise  in  crystal  imperfections,  leading  to  diminished 
crystallinity and potentially affecting electrical conductivity and magnetic behavior51. Conversely, the increase 
in  crystallite  size  with  Fe  doping  suggests  enhanced  structural  stability,  which  may  improve  the  material’s 
mechanical properties and reduce defect-related scattering, thereby optimizing its performance in applications 
like  catalysis  or  sensors.  Additionally,  the  alterations  in  lattice  parameters  due  to  ionic  radius  discrepancies 
highlight the significance of dopant selection on the overall structural integrity and functional characteristics 
of NiO 52.

Morphological studies
Morphological analyses, including grain size and surface morphology of pristine and doped NiO samples, were 
performed using FE-SEM. The consequence are illustrated in Fig. 4a-d. In all synthesized samples, the observation 
reveals minimal aggregation, random and homogeneous distribution, and roughly spherical grains along with 
the absence of defects and superior crystal quality53. This aggregation is a result of the nanoscale dimensions 
of  the  crystal  size,  as  smaller  nanocrystals  have  a  high  energy  of  surface45.  Furthermore,  the  aggregation  of 
metal  oxide  nanoparticles  is  a  compensation  mechanism  for  the  high  energy  of  surface  induced  by  the  high 
surface-to-volume ratio. Additionally, this random distribution is a result of the site selection of dopant ions 
on the surface of host materials. Conversely, doped NiO powders exhibit well-distributed and uniform grains. 
The presence of dopants within the NiO lattice influences the nucleation and growth process of NiO, thereby 
altering the morphology and size of the resulting samples. The dissymmetry in crystallite size may be attributed 
to the fusion of different crystallites, resulting in the formation of polycrystalline grains54. The incorporation of 
Cr and Cu ions into NiO leads to a reduction in grain size, indicating an increase in strain within the matrix 
and  a  limitation  in  lattice  growth.  All  synthesized  samples  exist  in  the  nanoscale  with  a  mean  size  range  of 
63–109 nm. This observation aligns with the anomalous nature of crystallite size as explained by XRD. Because, 
as seen in Table 1, the reduction of the interplanar distance (d) in nanoparticles leads to a decrease in the crystal 
dimensions (a = b = c) and an increase in the size of the crystallites46. On the other hand, with the increase in the 
size of the crystallites, the diameter of the nanoparticles (which are the result of the joining of several crystallites) 
observed in the FE-SEM shapes, also increases55. As a result, the agreement between XRD and FE-SEM results 
is confirmed for the samples under study.

Elemental evaluations
The  compositional  characterization  of  both  pristine  and  doped  NiO  nanoparticles  was  performed  utilizing 
Energy Dispersive Spectroscopy (EDS), with the resultant spectra illustrated in Fig. 5a-d. The EDS analysis of 
pristine NiO nanoparticles corroborates the presence of fundamental elemental constituents, specifically nickel 
(Ni) and oxygen (O). In contrast, the doped samples exhibit additional elemental signatures corresponding to 
the incorporation of dopants, including chromium (Cr), copper (Cu), and iron (Fe). The absence of extraneous

distinct peaks exclusively for Ni, O, and the respective doping elements, with no secondary peaks detected. This 
observation affirms that the synthesized powder in its pristine form is free from impurities, thereby validating 
the successful integration of dopants within the NiO matrix.

Using a high-intensity laser field, the refractive index of a nonlinear substance can be articulated as n = n₀ + n₂I,

linear and nonlinear absorption coefficients. When the sample is moved on the stage, photodiode (2) will detect

The results pertaining to pure nickel oxide (NiO) and its doped variants, namely copper (Cu), chromium (Cr), 
and  iron  (Fe)  are  illustrated  in  Fig.  8  and  9,  respectively. The  data  concerning  open  aperture  measurements, 
as shown in Fig. 9, indicate that the transmittance reaches a nadir at the focal point (z = 0), which signifies the 
presence of reverse saturable absorption (RSA) phenomena44,60. The trough observed in the nanostructures of 
Cu-doped  NiO,  Cr-doped  NiO,  and  Fe-doped  NiO  exhibits  a  notably  deeper  profile,  indicative  of  enhanced 
nonlinear  absorption  characteristics.  This  phenomenon  can  be  ascribed  to  processes  involving  excited-state 
absorption (ESA) and free carrier absorption (FCA). As a naturally occurring p-type semiconductor, NiO is 
characterized by a substantial band gap within its electronic structure. The incorporation of Cu, Cr, and Fe into 
NiO nanostructures engenders defect states, as corroborated by the associated absorption spectra. These defect 
states introduce intermediary energy levels within the band gap, thereby facilitating excited-state absorption. 
At a wavelength of 532 nm, negatively charged electrons that are excited from the lowest energy level become 
localized  in  these  intermediate  defect  states,  resulting  in  an  increase  in  photon  absorption  efficiency.  The 
subsequent release of energy occurs through non-radiative mechanisms, thereby enhancing the self-trapping of 
the excited state7,64. Moreover, the generation of electronic defect states in doped nickel oxide (NiO) becomes 
attainable through laser-induced excitation. The presence of copper (Cu), chromium (Cr), and iron (Fe) ions 
plays  a  crucial  role  in  trapping  the  electrons  produced  by  photon  interactions,  effectively  impeding  their 
recombination with positive holes. This process leads to an increased concentration of free charge carriers within 
the  doped  material.  In  semiconductor  physics,  free  carrier  absorption  (FCA)  is  a  recognized  phenomenon

Conclusion
Using  a  modified  co-precipitation  method,  NiO  nanoparticles  doped  with  Cu,  Cr,  and  Fe  were  successfully 
produced with a face-centered cubic structure. This study presents an effective co-precipitation method for the 
synthesis of x-doped NiO (with Cu, Cr, and Fe) nanopowders. The synthesized nanopowders were distinguished 
through  X-ray  diffraction  (XRD)  analysis,  which  revealed  that  they  possess  a  polycrystalline  cubic  structure 
with exhibited good crystallinity. As the substitution of Cr, Cu and Fe in the NiO, the size of the crystallites 
also reduced after the doping. Crystallite sizes measured were 84 nm for NiO, 77 nm for CuNiO, 63 nm for 
CrNiO, and 109 nm for FeNiO. XRD confirmed their structural integrity. The band gap energies were 3.09 eV, 
2.79 eV, 3.06 eV, and 3.18 eV for NiO, CuNiO, CrNiO, and FeNiO, consecutively, indicating band gap narrowing, 
excluding  FeNiO.  The  morphological  characteristics  of  the  nanoparticles  within  the  samples  were  validated 
through FE-SEM. The optical absorption spectra of the nanopowders were obtained via DRS in order to calculate 
the linear absorption coefficient (α0) pertinent to the operational wavelength of the Nd:YAG laser (532 nm). In
